  • The pill beside a step names its map, for example G-2. Point at it: for an item, a visit or a stay it says "Counts only in G-2"; for a kill or a flight it adds "or another company's x-2".
  • Patrols count outside safe zones only. Circling a gate's ring doesn't patrol a sector.
  • A kill counts for one level mission: the one you track, if it can use it, else the first of your active missions that can. Besides that it counts for every Challenge mission that asks for it, and every quest item step of yours that waits for that alien rolls its drop.
  • An alien a Company Pilot of yours finishes while you're fighting it counts as your kill, for your missions too.
  • A kill by someone in your group counts for your level missions too when you are on the same map and fired a laser or rocket at anything in the last 15 seconds. For the Challenge line the mate must also be within 4,000 units of the kill.

Time limits

  • Some missions are timed. Mission Control shows the limit on the mission's card before you accept it (a clock and "15 min"), and once you accept it a countdown runs on the card and in Active Quests. It turns amber in the last minute and red when time is up.
  • A timed mission that runs out fails: it leaves your active missions and you can accept it again at once, from the start.
  • The limits in the tables below are Alpha's. Beta's aliens are 1.5 times as strong and Gamma's twice, so their limits are 1.5 and 2 times as long. The clock is set when you accept the mission, for the world you're in.
  • Steps have no time limit of their own: the mission's limit covers all of them. A broken condition restarts a step or the mission, but it never resets the clock.

Rewards

  • Experience, credits, Thulium and honor are multiplied by the world the mission was done in: 1x in Alpha, 2x in Beta, 3x in Gamma. Your boosters (the Experience Booster, the Honor Booster) add to them, and premium doubles the experience. The Thulium and credits boosts of your clan add to the credits and the Thulium of every mission you claim: level, Station and Challenge.
  • Station and Challenge missions pay like level missions. The numbers printed in their tables are the base. A Challenge mission is paid by the world you did it in, like a level mission (the lowest one, should it span two). A Station mission has no world of its own: it pays the world you fly in when you claim it.
  • An example. Seeker Plague (Challenge) has a base of 1,100,000 credits, 8,260 Thulium, 157,500 XP and 3,060 honor. Done and claimed in Gamma with nothing switched on, it pays 3,300,000 credits, 24,780 Thulium, 472,500 XP and 9,180 honor. With your clan's Credits and Thulium boosts at their top (+10% each) it pays 3,630,000 credits and 27,258 Thulium.
  • The clan bank cap. However big a claim is, a pilot can send at most 1,000,000 credits into clans in any 24 hours.
  • Items and booster time are the same in every world. Items go to your inventory, booster hours add to what the booster has left, and ammo is ready to fire even if you claim while flying.
  • Items are Marketable. What a mission pays in items (gear, ammo, rockets, materials, Reinforced Plates) can be sold on the Auction from level 5. The Challenge missions pay no gear: their items are materials and Reinforced Plates.

The reworked missions

Update 0.4.10 reworked the level missions into chains. 64 of the 88 are new versions; the 24 that stayed as they were are the plain kill missions (like Basic Training: Combat) and the Specials of levels 1, 2 and 5 to 8.

If you had done one of the 64, you do the new version too. At your first flight after the update a System line tells you: "Mission Control has new missions: the level quests were reworked."

  • The mission is offered again. It is back in Mission Control, and it pays its full reward again: experience, credits, Thulium, honor and items, by the world you do it in.
  • A Special locks again until the level's regular missions are done again, so level 3's ten missions come before Hive Breaker once more.
  • A reward you had not claimed yet is paid as before (the larger of the old and the new reward), and then the new version is offered.
  • A mission you had running is carried over to its new steps by the share you had done. A visit counts only when its share is whole, and a quest item is never handed in by that conversion.
  • Nothing goes down. Your level, your statistics and your Wipe Points stay. A mission you do again does not count for the Wipe Points a second time: it was counted the first time.
  • The Station missions, the Challenge line and the 24 missions that stayed are not touched.

Danger

The higher sectors are where the missions pay, and where you can die. Plan your kit for them:

  • PvP: other companies' pilots can attack you in x-4 and the centre in every world, from x-2 up in Beta, and everywhere in Gamma (except in safe zones and during the Peace Protocol). The ring gates bring other companies' pilots into your x-3 too: in Beta and Gamma one of them can destroy you there while you carry an item.
  • Bulwarks (x-3, x-4) outrun a Protos and hit hard. Fight them from an Ostirion, near a gate's safe zone, and pull back into it to repair.
  • Goombahs (x-3, x-4) have a range of 800, hit for 3,000 and never start a fight: leave one alone and it leaves you alone, shoot it and it turns on you until 10 seconds after your last hit (and it mends when left alone). A ship whose lasers are all Starfire-III (range 850) outranges them and Bulwarks alike: with a ship faster than they are (an Ostirion or above; a Goombah flies 180, a Bulwark 175) you can fire without taking a hit. Your ship's range is the average of its lasers' ranges, so a Starfire-III beside two Quantum Laser II fires from 750: far enough to keep away from a Bulwark (700), not from a Goombah (800). Level 5's Special gives you one; you can also make one in Assembly, from Velkonite Reinforced Plates that the Forgery of your Skylab makes.
  • Crystalys roam the border (x-4). Nothing in reach of level 8 outranges one, and only a fast ship outruns it: keep your distance, and watch the minimap.
  • When you are destroyed you choose where to come back: at your base, at the nearest portal or on the spot (see Dying and Coming Back). A timed mission's clock keeps running meanwhile, a carried item is lost, and a no-death rule breaks.

The missions

The time limits are Alpha's ("–": none). "→" joins the steps of an In order mission, which must be done in that order; steps joined by ";" open together and can be done in any order. A condition written after a step belongs to that step, "(whole mission: ...)" to every step.

A quest item reads "may drop it: 15% a kill, for certain at kill 10": every kill of that alien in that sector rolls the chance, and the 10th kill since the step opened drops it for sure. "From season day 4" is a swarm hunt.

# Quests

Missions are the main way to level up. Mission Control hands them out: every mission comes from an officer of your own company (if you [change company](/wiki/01-General/Getting-Started.md#changing-your-company), the officers become your new company's, and the `rival x-4` tasks follow it), and each pays experience, credits, Thulium and honor when you claim it. There are **88 missions for levels 1 to 8**, eleven a level, and together they carry you from a fresh Protos to the frontline of the PvP centre. Ten **Station missions** teach you the [Skylab](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Skylab.md) and pay you for building it up, and from pilot level 3 a separate line of fifty very hard **Challenge missions** pays large rewards. Station and Challenge missions pay like the level missions: the numbers in the tables are the **base**, and your world, boosters and clan boosts multiply them ([Rewards](#rewards)).

Most missions are no longer "destroy so many of these": they are short **chains**. You destroy a few aliens, fly to a point, stay in a sector for some minutes, or find an item and drive it home to Mission Control. Some add a rule: lose no more than so many hull points, or do not die.

---

![Mission Control with the Challenges tab and the Active Quests window](../img/wiki-img/shots/mission-control-challenges.jpg)
![Quest points around the ship: a private item, a placed one, a visit point and the delivery ring](../img/wiki-img/shots/quest-points.jpg)

## In one minute

- **Take them at Mission Control.** You can run 5 level missions at once, plus 3 Station missions and 3 Challenge missions.
- **Chains.** The steps of a mission with an **In order** tag open one after the other, and only the open step counts.
- **Four kinds of step besides kills.** A **quest item** that drops only for you and that you drive to Mission Control, a **point to visit**, a **stay** of some minutes in a sector and, from season day 4, a **swarm** to hunt.
- **Conditions.** A step or a whole mission may say "hull loss at most N points" or "no death". Break it and that step, or the mission, starts again. Nothing is lost for good.
- **The Challenge line.** Fifty very hard missions in five tiers of ten, from pilot level 3. They pay by the work: a kill is worth what tier I pays for it, and 10% more for every tier up, and one claim pays at most 100,000 Thulium. Tier I pays 9,355,000 credits, 70,125 Thulium and 2,177,500 XP in all, as base values ([The Challenge line](#challenge-line)).
- **Reworked in 0.4.10.** 64 of the level missions are new versions. If you had done one, it is offered again, with its full reward ([details](#reworked-missions)).

## Mission Control



- Open **Mission Control** from the toolbar inside a station's safe zone, or click the **Mission Control** bubble above the station in your base sector (it follows the station on the map, so fly or zoom out until the station is in view). The **Normal Missions** tab lists your missions by level, the **Challenges** tab holds the [Challenge line](#challenge-line), and **Completed Missions** holds the ones waiting for you to claim their reward.
- **Accept** a mission to start it. You can run **5 missions at once**; the [Station missions](#station-missions) have 3 slots of their own and the [Challenge missions](#challenge-line) 3 more. The mission you accepted last is the one you're **tracking** (a Station mission only when you track nothing and none of your missions is one that flying can advance): it shows in the **Active Quests** window, and kills and flight count toward it first. Pick another with the dots in the window's title bar.
- A **badge** with a count sits on the Mission Control button, and on its **Normal Missions** and **Challenges** tabs while you are on another tab, as long as a mission or a Challenge can be accepted. Each new one comes with one toast and a quiet sound.
- Some missions must be done **in order**. They carry an **In order** tag, and their steps are numbered: see [Chained missions](#chained-missions).
- A mission with a quest item, a stay or a condition shows its state live in Active Quests: **Carrying** with the distance to Mission Control, the time you have stayed, the hull points you have lost (**Hull damage: 1,240 / 3,000**), **Do not die**. On the mission's card the same rules show as small pills: **Hull limit 3,000 HP**, **No death**, **In order**, and the clock of a timed mission.
- **Abandon** a mission to drop it and its progress. It is back in the list at once, and you can take it again. An item you were carrying for it is gone.
- A finished mission waits under **Completed Missions** until you **claim** it. Claim it whenever you like: the reward doesn't expire.
- Every mission can be done **once per pilot**, except the level missions that were reworked in 0.4.10, which are offered once more ([see below](#reworked-missions)). Your missions, done and in progress, survive the season's wipe.

## Levels

- Each level from 1 to 8 has **ten missions and a Special**. A level's missions open when you reach it and stay open at every level above it.
- **Take them in any order.** None of the ten waits for another. (The steps inside one mission may have an order.)
- Every level has the same mix: **three** missions with a quest item, **two** that send you to points on the map, **two** that make you stay in a sector and **three** plain hunts. A mission has one to four steps, and a hunt asks for one kind of alien or for several.
- The missions of a level pay **85% of the experience** to the next level. The aliens they have you destroy pay the rest, and at low levels quite a bit more: you usually reach the next level before a set is finished.
- **One Asteroids mission for each level.** Besides its ten and the Special, every level has a mission that asks you to break a number of [asteroids](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Asteroid-Mining.md) of kinds that live on better maps as the levels rise (the first pays 60 Rivet I; those of levels 7 and 8 open on season day 4). A break counts when it pays you a share (at least 5% of the damage the asteroid takes), with rockets or lasers. It is not one of the ten, so the Special does not wait for it, but it takes one of your 5 mission slots. Mission Control lists it after the Special, marked **Asteroids**; the tables at the end of this page do not.

## Special missions

- The eleventh mission of each level is its **Special**. It is locked until **all ten** of the level's other missions are done (claimed, or waiting for their claim), and its card says how many you have left.
- Specials pay more experience than any other mission of their level, and **items** besides: lasers, shield parts, generators, Power Cores, Ship Fragments, ammo and booster time.
- The Specials of levels 3 and 4, **Hive Breaker** and **Hive Purge**, are [swarm hunts](#swarm-missions): they open from season day 4.
- Level 1's regular missions also give a small starter item each: a Light Shield Core, a Repair Drone, a Damage Amp I, an Absorption Shield Cell I, some ammo and a stack of rockets to try each kind (Lancet I, Rivet I, Ember I and Scatter I, and Lancet II from the Special).

## Chained missions

A **chain** is a mission whose steps go in a fixed order. It carries an **In order** tag on its card and in Active Quests. Its steps are numbered: a done step is checked, the **highlighted** step is the open one, and the steps after it show a lock until it is done.

- **Only the open step counts.** Your kills, your flight and your stay time go to it and to no other. Kills you made before a step opened do not count for it.
- **Why in order?** A mission tells a small story ("clear the guards, then take the core home"), and the rules need the order: a quest item can only drop once its step is open, a stay counts from the moment it opens, and the conditions of a step (hull limit, no death) run only while that step is open.
- **Missions without the tag open all their steps at once**, in any order. **Hold the Gate** has a point to reach, a four-minute stay in one stretch and kills of 8 Seekers and 3 Phantasm, all open together, so the kills count whenever you make them while the mission runs, in the stay or out of it.
- In the tables at the end of this page an arrow ("→") joins the steps of an In order mission, and a semicolon (";") joins steps that open together.

## Quest items

A quest item is something you have to bring to Mission Control. It is not an inventory item: it cannot be traded, stored or sold, it is part of the mission. **Only you can see it.** Other pilots, your group mates too, see nothing.

| Kind | How you get it | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **A drop** | Every kill of the named alien in the named sector may drop it. The table gives the chance a kill ("15% a kill") and the kill that drops it for certain ("for certain at kill 10"). The count starts when the step opens. | Combined Operations: the Cargo Pod, from the Seekers of `x-1`. |
| **A scripted drop** | No chance: the named kill, counted from the moment the step opens, always carries it. | Nest Raid: the third Phantasm of the nest carries the Nest Core. |
| **A placed item** | It lies at a point of the sector from the moment the step opens. | Frontier Defense: the Relay Part at 12,500 / 4,800 in `x-2`. |

1. **Find it.** A drop appears where the alien died, for **120 seconds**; it blinks in the last 12. If you miss it, the next qualifying kill drops it again at once. You see the item as a cyan beacon in the world (a spinning data core in a ring, with a beam rising from it) and as a cyan diamond on the minimap.
2. **Pick it up.** Fly within **200 units** of it. A message says it is on board, and Active Quests shows **Carrying** and the distance to Mission Control.
3. **Drive it home.** Fly into the safe zone of **your own company's** Mission Control: the station of your base sector `x-1`, the ring of 1,600 units around it. A green ring on the screen and on the minimap shows it. The item is delivered at once and the step is done.

Things that stop the carry:

- **Your ship is destroyed**, by an alien or by a pilot: the item is lost, and you can get it again (a placed item is back at its point, a drop comes with the next qualifying kill). Nobody can steal it: a pilot who destroys you gets nothing from it.
- **A passed hull limit** or a **no death** rule fails the carry the same way: see [Conditions](#conditions).
- **The Jump CPU and the Base CPU refuse to work while you carry an item.** Fly home through the gates. Gates, the cloak and Shield Surge are free to use.
- If you leave the game you keep carrying when you come back. A drop that was standing on the map is gone, and the next qualifying kill drops it again.
- Items are only ever in the company sectors `x-1` to `x-4`, **never in the Danger Sectors**, and only in **your own company's**: a Galactic pilot's item lies on `G-2`, never on `M-2` or `T-2`. An alien drops your item only when it dies in your own company's sector.
- In a [group](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Groups.md) every mate who counts for the kill (see [Where it counts](#where-it-counts)) and has the mission rolls and sees their own item. Nobody can give, take or share one.

> [!TIP]
> Plan the way home before you pick the item up. From `x-3` or `x-4` it is two gate jumps to `x-1`, from `x-2` one. Mend first if your hull is low (a destroyed ship loses the item) and keep out of fights on the way: repairs do not give hull-limit points back.

## Visit and stay

**Visit a point.** A visit step names a point of a sector as two numbers, "9,000 / 4,500". They are the same numbers the title bar of the minimap shows for your own ship, so you can steer by them. Fly within **400 units** of the point and it counts at once; you do not have to stop (a tour that ends at Mission Control ends inside the station's safe zone). The point is a **gold ring** on the screen and a gold diamond on the minimap. It counts only on your own company's map, not in the same sector of another company.

**Stay in a sector.** A stay step asks for some minutes in a sector. It counts only while all three are true:

- you are on the sector the step names (for an `x-n`, your own company's map);
- you are **outside every safe zone** (a station's or a gate's ring: time in a ring does not count);
- your ship is **active**: it has flown 300 units or fired a shot in the last 30 seconds. A parked ship earns nothing.

There are two kinds. A stay that **adds up** keeps what you have: leave, die, come back, and the minutes are still there, unless the stay or its mission has a hull limit or a no-death rule: then losing your ship or passing the limit starts the stay again (see [Conditions](#conditions)). A stay **in one stretch** starts again from zero when you die, jump or leave the sector (time in a ring or standing still only pauses it), and a toast says so.

Stays and visits do not compete: every open one counts at once, whatever else you are doing. Kills are different: a kill counts for one level mission only (see [Where it counts](#where-it-counts)).

> [!NOTE]
> Visits and stays may lead into the Danger Sectors (Centre Recon, Centre Vigil and Centre Hold do), where other companies' pilots can attack you. Quest items never do. A visit point in `DS-x` counts in any Danger Sector: from season day 11 do the points near the top-left corner of `DS-4`, such as the corner of **Four Corners**, in `DS-1`, `DS-2` or `DS-3`, because that corner of `DS-4` is inside the guns of the [Dormant Swamp](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Dormant-Swamp.md).

## Swarm missions

Thirteen missions ask for the ships of the [swarms](/wiki/05-Swarms/Swarms.md). Two are level Specials: **Hive Breaker** (level 3: 3 Boss Seekers, 12 Seeker Slaves and 6 Phantasm) and **Hive Purge** (level 4: 3 Boss Seekers, 12 Seeker Slaves, 2 Bulwarks and a point to visit). Eleven are in the Challenge line: Boss Seekers and Pirate Scouts (**Hive Cull**, **Scout Cull**, **Hive Culling II**, **Scout Culling II**), Pirate Bosses (**Pirate Reckoning**, **Pirate Bane**, **Pirate Doom**, **Pirate Throne**) and the Dormant Force (**Dormant Dawn**, **Dormant Dusk**, **Dormant Dominion**).

- **They open on season day 4**, the day the swarms appear ([30-day schedule](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Wipe-Timeline.md#30-day-season-schedule)). Before it Mission Control refuses them with "This mission opens on season day 4".
- A swarm ship counts under **its own name**: a Boss Seeker or a Seeker Slave is no Seeker, a Pirate Scout is no Phantasm.
- The step names no sector, because the swarms roam: the [Seeker Swarm](/wiki/05-Swarms/Seeker-Swarm.md) in `x-1` and `x-2`, the [Pirate Swarm](/wiki/05-Swarms/Pirate-Swarm.md) in `x-2` and `x-3`, the [Dormant Swarm](/wiki/05-Swarms/Dormant-Swarm.md) in the Danger Sectors. A Boss Seeker or a Pirate Boss comes back 2 minutes after it falls. From season day 11 the Dormant Swarm starts at the [Dormant Swamp](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Dormant-Swamp.md).
- The Dormant missions are for a crew: there is one Dormant Swarm in each world, and a group of strong ships takes it ([how the fight goes](/wiki/05-Swarms/Dormant-Swarm.md#how-the-fight-goes)). The next tier does not wait for **Dormant Dawn** or **Dormant Dusk** ([the Challenge line](#challenge-line)).
- A Boss Seeker hits harder than a new pilot's ship can bear: read [how the fight goes](/wiki/05-Swarms/Seeker-Swarm.md#how-the-fight-goes) before you start.

## Conditions

A **condition** is an extra rule on one step or on a whole mission. There are two. The tables write them as "(hull loss at most 3,000 points)" and "(no death)"; a condition on the whole mission reads "(whole mission: ...)".

- **Hull limit.** Lose no more than so many **hull points**. The count is the hull you really lose: the points the hull bar falls by, after your shield and absorbance have taken their share. Damage to the shield does not count, black-hole radiation does, and repairs give nothing back. A killing blow always passes the limit.
- **No death.** If your ship is destroyed, the condition breaks.

**When the clock runs.** A limit on a whole mission counts from the moment you accept it (and from every restart) until the mission is done. A limit on a step counts from the moment the step opens; for a carried item, from the pick-up to the delivery. It counts every hull point you lose in that time, whoever hits you, and in a mission whose steps are open together that includes the fights of its other steps.

**What a broken condition does.** Nothing is lost for good, no Thulium is charged and the mission stays active. A message tells you ("condition broken. The attempt starts again.").

| What carries the condition | What happens when it breaks |
| :--- | :--- |
| A kill step | The kills of that step go back to 0. The other steps keep their progress. |
| A carried item | The carry fails and you fetch the item again (see [Quest items](#quest-items)). |
| A visit or a stay step | The step starts again. |
| A whole mission | Every step starts again, a carried item is lost, and the clock of a timed mission keeps running. |

Dying breaks a hull limit that is running as well as a no-death rule.

The limits are set in points, for the ship you fly at that level. A carried item's limit is 3,000 hull points on levels 1 to 3, 17,000 on levels 4 to 6 and 46,000 on levels 7 and 8; stays and tours that run longer have larger numbers. They are the same in every world, so in Beta and Gamma, where the aliens hit harder, they leave you less room. Check the mission's card before you accept. A limit may also be given as a percent of your ship's hull, and the stricter one counts when both are given; every mission of this release uses points.

## Mission examples

Eight missions from the real list, from the first hour to the Challenge line. Their numbers are in the tables at the end of this page; every pay named here is the **base** (see [Rewards](#rewards)).

- **Beacon Watch** (level 1). Fly to the point 9,000 / 4,500 in `x-1`, then stay 5 minutes in `x-1`. The whole mission is **no death**: if your ship is destroyed, you begin again at the beacon. Keep moving or shooting, or the minutes do not count. Pays 700 XP, 3,500 credits, 5 Thulium, 7 honor and a Repair Drone I.
- **Combined Operations** (level 1). Destroy 8 Seekers in `x-1`, then find the Cargo Pod: every Seeker you destroy there after that has a 15% chance to carry it, and the 10th is sure. Bring it to Mission Control with a hull loss of at most 3,000 points. Pays 1,550 XP, 8,000 credits, Advanced Plasma and Ember I.
- **Hold the Gate** (level 2, 15 minutes, no death). Four steps open at once: reach the point 12,500 / 2,500 in `x-2`, stay 4 minutes in one stretch there, and destroy 8 Seekers and 3 Phantasm. The kills count whenever you make them while the mission runs. Die, and everything starts again, but the clock does not.
- **Nest Raid** (level 3). Pays 10,500 XP, 52,000 credits and 315 Thulium.
- **Hive Breaker** (level 3 Special, from season day 4). Destroy 3 Boss Seekers and 12 Seeker Slaves, in any sector, and 6 Phantasm in `x-3`, in any order. Pays 6,800 XP, 54,500 credits, 170 Thulium, a Quantum Laser II, 10 Ship Fragments and 200 Ultra Core.

## Station missions

- Ten missions about your [Skylab](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Skylab.md), in a **Station** section at the top of the Missions page. The first, **Light the Station**, is open from level 1 and tells you where the Skylab is: Menu, Economy, Skylab. The station menu's Skylab row pulses until you have taken it or built Solar.
- They are taken, tracked, abandoned and claimed like every mission, but they don't count in the 5: you can run **3 Station missions at once** besides your other 5. A Station mission can wait for hours of upgrade timers and never holds up a combat mission.
- Taking a Station mission doesn't change the mission you're tracking when you have one that flying can advance: the Active Quests window keeps showing your combat mission, and the Station mission is a dot in its title bar (hover it for its progress, click it to show it).
- Each opens at its own **pilot level** and after the Station missions it follows (claimed first): a locked card says which. The first three open at level 1. The last, **Core Ten**, takes the Core to level 10, the level that opens the Skylab's [Research Centre](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Research.md).
- Their tasks read your Skylab: **build** a module or **raise it to a level** (done while the module is at that level or higher; no module goes above your Core, so a Solar goal can need the Core raised first), and **collect** credits from the Credit Farm (counted from the moment you accept the mission, with the Collect Resources button). A mission whose tasks are all true at once is done: one you already meet when you accept it is done at once.
- The Credit Farm costs nothing to build, so **First Farm** pays you 3,000 Credits and 100 Thulium for building it. Collecting takes time: **Payday** asks for 1,000 Credits, about an hour and a half of a level 1 farm (750 an hour), and **Fifty Thousand** asks for 50,000, about 22 hours of the level 3 farm that **Growing Season** leaves you (2,250 an hour).
- Solar makes only 25% of its power while it upgrades, so a station with a Thulium Farm stops its farms until the upgrade is done (see [Solar Module](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Skylab.md#solar-module)). **Brighter Panels** (Solar to level 3: 5 and 15 minutes; the small station of that mission still fits), **Growing Season** (the step to level 5 takes 45 minutes) and **Open the Supply Line** (Solar to level 6: 60 minutes) tell you how long it lasts.
- **They pay like a level mission.** The numbers in the table are the **base**: your world's bonus, boosters, Premium XP and your clan's Credits and Thulium boosts multiply them ([Rewards](#rewards)). A Station mission has no world of its own, so it pays the world you fly in when you claim it. It gives no items. Their base experience is on top of the 85% the levels' missions pay (at most 5% of a level's gap).
- Station missions don't count toward the [Wipe Points](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Wipe-Timeline.md) for missions done. They survive the wipe like every mission, and so does what you built.

## The Challenge line {#challenge-line}

From **pilot level 3**, the **Challenges** tab of Mission Control opens a second line: **fifty very hard missions in five tiers of ten**, for the pilots who want more than the levels give. Every tier asks for more than the one before, and all fifty are in the game. [The tables](#challenge-missions-table) at the end of this page list every mission and every number.

- **Ten in any order.** The ten missions of a tier are open together. **Tier II** opens when you have claimed all ten of tier I, and **tier III** when you have claimed all ten of tier II. **Tiers IV and V** open when you have claimed **nine of the ten** before them: **Dormant Dawn** (tier III) and **Dormant Dusk** (tier IV) are missions of the [Dormant Swarm](/wiki/05-Swarms/Dormant-Swarm.md), which needs a crew, so they are optional.
- **Three at once**, besides your 5 level missions and 3 Station missions.
- **They pay like a level mission.** The reward in the tables is the **base**, paid once: your world's bonus, boosters, Premium XP and your clan's Credits and Thulium boosts multiply it, as [Rewards](#rewards) explains with an example. **Honor is paid in tier I only.** They survive the wipe, and they do not count for the Wipe Points of missions.
- **The pay follows the work.** In a Challenge one kill of an alien kind is worth what tier I pays for it, and **10% more in every tier up** (tier II ×1.10, tier III ×1.21, tier IV ×1.331, tier V ×1.4641). So the 150 Bulwarks of **Bulwark Wall** pay 19,585 Thulium in tier I, and the 400 of **Bulwark Storm** in tier II pay 57,450: a Bulwark is worth 10% more there. Stays, tours and clean runs follow the same rule against the mission of their own kind one tier below.
- **A ceiling of 100,000 Thulium a claim.** The biggest hunts would pay more. When a claim comes to more than 100,000 Thulium, the whole claim is cut down together until its Thulium is exactly 100,000: credits, honor and items shrink in the same proportion. Ten missions are cut: **Goombah Scourge**, **Bulwark Blight**, **Goombah Rout**, **Bulwark Sea**, **Ten Thousand Seekers**, **Ten Thousand Phantasm**, **Goombah Legion**, **Crystalys Reign**, **Pirate Throne** and **Warden of the Line**. The other forty pay in full.
- **Experience: five times.** The experience of all fifty missions is exactly 5 times what they paid before 0.4.16, whatever the ceiling cuts.
- **The items grow with the money.** Power Cores, Reinforced Hull Plates and Cataclysite grow with the credits and Thulium of the claim. The Orvium and Velkonite Reinforced Plates and the Ancient Control Units stay at their old quantities, and the booster hours are the same.
- **Your kills pay on top.** The aliens you destroy still pay their own credits, Thulium and honor as ever; the claim comes in addition to that.
- **Kills count twice.** A kill counts for every Challenge mission that asks for it **and** for the one level mission it counts for, so a thousand-kill mission never starves your level missions.
- **Groups.** A kill counts for the pilot who is paid for it and for every group mate within **4,000 units** of the wreck who fired a laser or a rocket in the last 15 seconds. Each pilot keeps their own count.
- **Stays need shots, except in the centre.** A stay in `x-3`, in `x-4` or in a rival's `x-4` counts only while you have fired a shot in the last 60 seconds, so a parked or circling ship earns nothing. The stays in the Danger Sectors (**Centre Watch**, **Rim Vigil**, **Last Watch**), where no ordinary alien lives (the aliens that wake from season day 11, see [Danger Sectors](/wiki/01-General/Danger-Sectors.md), do not change the rule), count a ship that has flown 300 units or fired in the last 30 seconds, as the stays of the level missions do.

## Where it counts

Most steps name the sector where they count, and only kills and distance flown **there** count toward them. A visit, a stay and an item name their sector the same way, but they are stricter: they count only on **your own company's** map. An item that a mission puts in `G-2` lies on `G-2` and nowhere else, and a Galactic pilot finds nothing of it on Mars' `M-2` or Terra's `T-2`. Kills and distance flown count in that sector of any company. A few kill steps name none and count in **every** sector: the swarm ships of Hive Breaker and Hive Purge, and the big hunts of the Challenge line (Seeker Plague, Phantasm Tide, Bulwark Wall, Hive Cull, Scout Cull and the big hunts of the tiers after tier I). The Station steps read your Skylab and have no sector either. The sector shows next to a step as one of your own maps:

| In the tables | Means | You see (a Mars pilot) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `x-1` … `x-4` | for kills and distance flown: that sector of any company, yours or another company's; for an item, a visit and a stay: your own company's sector only | `M-3` |
| `DS-x` | any sector of the PvP centre, the Danger Sectors `DS-1` to `DS-4` | `DS-x` |
| `rival x-4` | another company's border sector (not yours), a short hop through the ring gates or across the centre | `T-4 · G-4` |

The missions climb the sectors with your level:

| Level | Where you fight | Where it leads |
| --: | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | your base (`x-1`) and second sector (`x-2`) | – |
| 2 | the second sector | a first look through the gate into `x-3` |
| 3 | the third sector (`x-3`), near its gate; a few warm-ups in `x-2` | – |
| 4 | the third sector | a look through the border gate into `x-4` |
| 5 | the third sector | the first crossings of the border (`x-4`) |
| 6 | the border (`x-4`) | – |
| 7 | the border | runs into the PvP centre (`DS-x`) |
| 8 | the border | the centre, and other companies' borders |

- **The pill beside a step** names its map, for example `G-2`. Point at it: for an item, a visit or a stay it says "Counts only in G-2"; for a kill or a flight it adds "or another company's `x-2`".
- **Patrols count outside safe zones only.** Circling a gate's ring doesn't patrol a sector.
- **A kill counts for one level mission**: the one you track, if it can use it, else the first of your active missions that can. Besides that it counts for every Challenge mission that asks for it, and every quest item step of yours that waits for that alien rolls its drop.
- An alien a [Company Pilot](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Company-Pilots.md) of yours finishes while you're fighting it counts as your kill, for your missions too.
- A kill by someone in your [group](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Groups.md) counts for your level missions too when you are on the same map and fired a laser or rocket at anything in the last 15 seconds. For the Challenge line the mate must also be within 4,000 units of the kill.

## Time limits

- Some missions are **timed**. Mission Control shows the limit on the mission's card before you accept it (a clock and "15 min"), and once you accept it a **countdown** runs on the card and in Active Quests. It turns amber in the last minute and red when time is up.
- A timed mission that runs out **fails**: it leaves your active missions and you can accept it again at once, from the start.
- The limits in the tables below are **Alpha's**. Beta's aliens are 1.5 times as strong and Gamma's twice, so their limits are 1.5 and 2 times as long. The clock is set when you accept the mission, for the world you're in.
- Steps have no time limit of their own: the mission's limit covers all of them. A broken condition restarts a step or the mission, but it never resets the clock.

## Rewards

- Experience, credits, Thulium and honor are multiplied by the [world](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Wipe-Timeline.md#worlds-alpha-beta-and-gamma) the mission was done in: 1x in Alpha, 2x in Beta, 3x in Gamma. Your boosters (the Experience Booster, the Honor Booster) add to them, and premium doubles the experience. The Thulium and credits boosts of your [clan](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Clans.md) add to the credits and the Thulium of every mission you claim: level, Station and Challenge.
- **Station and Challenge missions pay like level missions.** The numbers printed in their tables are the **base**. A Challenge mission is paid by the world you did it in, like a level mission (the lowest one, should it span two). A Station mission has no world of its own: it pays the world you fly in when you claim it.
- **An example.** **Seeker Plague** (Challenge) has a base of 1,100,000 credits, 8,260 Thulium, 157,500 XP and 3,060 honor. Done and claimed in Gamma with nothing switched on, it pays 3,300,000 credits, 24,780 Thulium, 472,500 XP and 9,180 honor. With your clan's Credits and Thulium boosts at their top (+10% each) it pays 3,630,000 credits and 27,258 Thulium.
- **The clan bank cap.** However big a claim is, a pilot can send at most 1,000,000 credits into [clans](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Clans.md#2-donations) in any 24 hours.
- **Items and booster time are the same in every world.** Items go to your inventory, booster hours add to what the booster has left, and ammo is ready to fire even if you claim while flying.
- **Items are Marketable.** What a mission pays in items (gear, ammo, rockets, materials, Reinforced Plates) can be sold on the [Auction](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Auction.md#marketable-items) from level 5. The Challenge missions pay no gear: their items are materials and Reinforced Plates.

## The reworked missions {#reworked-missions}

Update 0.4.10 reworked the level missions into chains. **64 of the 88 are new versions**; the 24 that stayed as they were are the plain kill missions (like Basic Training: Combat) and the Specials of levels 1, 2 and 5 to 8.

If you had **done** one of the 64, you do the new version too. At your first flight after the update a System line tells you: "Mission Control has new missions: the level quests were reworked."

- **The mission is offered again.** It is back in Mission Control, and it pays its **full reward** again: experience, credits, Thulium, honor and items, by the world you do it in.
- **A Special locks again** until the level's regular missions are done again, so level 3's ten missions come before Hive Breaker once more.
- **A reward you had not claimed yet** is paid as before (the larger of the old and the new reward), and then the new version is offered.
- **A mission you had running** is carried over to its new steps by the share you had done. A visit counts only when its share is whole, and a quest item is never handed in by that conversion.
- **Nothing goes down.** Your level, your statistics and your Wipe Points stay. A mission you do again does not count for the [Wipe Points](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Wipe-Timeline.md#earning-wipe-points) a second time: it was counted the first time.
- The Station missions, the Challenge line and the 24 missions that stayed are not touched.

## Danger

The higher sectors are where the missions pay, and where you can die. Plan your kit for them:

- **PvP**: other companies' pilots can attack you in `x-4` and the centre in every world, from `x-2` up in Beta, and everywhere in Gamma (except in safe zones and during the Peace Protocol). The ring gates bring other companies' pilots into your `x-3` too: in Beta and Gamma one of them can destroy you there while you carry an item.
- **Bulwarks** (`x-3`, `x-4`) outrun a Protos and hit hard. Fight them from an [Ostirion](/wiki/02-Ships/Ostirion.md), near a gate's safe zone, and pull back into it to repair.
- **Goombahs** (`x-3`, `x-4`) have a range of 800, hit for 3,000 and never start a fight: leave one alone and it leaves you alone, shoot it and it turns on you until 10 seconds after your last hit (and it mends when left alone). A ship whose lasers are all [Starfire-III](/wiki/06-Items/Lasers.md) (range 850) outranges them and Bulwarks alike: with a ship faster than they are (an Ostirion or above; a Goombah flies 180, a Bulwark 175) you can fire without taking a hit. Your ship's range is the average of its lasers' ranges, so a Starfire-III beside two Quantum Laser II fires from 750: far enough to keep away from a Bulwark (700), not from a Goombah (800). Level 5's Special gives you one; you can also make one in Assembly, from Velkonite Reinforced Plates that the Forgery of your [Skylab](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Skylab.md) makes.
- **Crystalys** roam the border (`x-4`). Nothing in reach of level 8 outranges one, and only a fast ship outruns it: keep your distance, and watch the minimap.
- When you are destroyed you choose where to come back: at your base, at the nearest portal or on the spot (see [Dying and Coming Back](/wiki/01-General/Getting-Started.md)). A timed mission's clock keeps running meanwhile, a carried item is lost, and a no-death rule breaks.

## The missions

The time limits are Alpha's ("–": none). "→" joins the steps of an **In order** mission, which must be done in that order; steps joined by ";" open together and can be done in any order. A condition written after a step belongs to that step, "(whole mission: ...)" to every step.

A quest item reads "may drop it: 15% a kill, for certain at kill 10": every kill of that alien in that sector rolls the chance, and the 10th kill since the step opened drops it for sure. "From season day 4" is a [swarm hunt](#swarm-missions).

ranks.html:
Every pilot has a rank, from Junior Pilot to Senior Admiral. It is a military ladder of 8 tiers with 3 grades each, 24 ranks in all. Your rank comes from your PvE points: the points you earn from your level, your experience and the aliens you destroy. Every rank asks for a minimum of PvE points, and the six best ranks also have a fixed number of places in each company. In flight the game shows only a small symbol before a pilot's name, so you can tell the best pilots of a company from a fresh one at a glance, and one pilot of the whole server wears a gold crown over his symbol. The words are on the Company page and in the hover tip of a symbol.

In one minute

  • Your company keeps one list of its pilots, the pilot with the most PvE points first. Every company has its own, and the pilots of the other companies never count against you.
  • You hold the highest rank whose minimum your points reach and that still has a place free in your company.
  • The six best ranks have a number of places per company: Senior Admiral 1 (from 50,000 PvE points), Admiral 2 (from 45,000), Junior Admiral 4 (from 40,000), Senior General 8 (from 30,000), General 10 (from 27,500) and Junior General 15 (from 25,000). The ranks below have no limit on pilots, and each asks 2,500 points less than the rank above it, down to the 2,500 of a Junior Captain.
  • Equal points, equal rank. Two pilots with the same points never hold different ranks. When the last place of a rank falls inside a tie, the tied pilots all take the better rank, even if that goes over its places.
  • Only pilots with PvE points who flew in the last 30 days are on a list. Everybody else is a Junior Pilot until they fly again, and holds no place.
  • A gold crown over the symbol marks the pilot with the most PvE points of the whole server: every company, all three worlds.
  • Your rank moves. Up to Senior Colonel it depends on your points alone, so it only rises. The six best ranks also move with the other pilots of your company: they can fall when others take the places above you. A fall is never announced; a new best rank is.
  • The wipe does not change anybody's points, so the lists do not start over.
  • The symbol before a name is the rank: a shape for the tier, one to three marks for the grade.

The company ladder

The pilots of your company, all three worlds together, stand in one line, the pilot with the most PvE points first. This line is the ladder. When two pilots have the same points, the one with the higher level is listed first, then the older pilot, but that only sets the order of the list: it never gives them different ranks. Your rank comes from two things, your points and the places of your company:

  1. Every rank has a minimum of PvE points (the table below). A pilot never holds a rank whose minimum his points have not reached.
  2. The six best ranks have places. They are filled from the top, the best rank first: the best pilots who reach 50,000 points are the Senior Admirals, up to the one place; of the pilots left, the best who reach 45,000 are the Admirals, up to their two places; and so on down to the Junior Generals.
  3. Everybody else holds the highest rank his points reach below those six, which is a Senior Colonel at best. A pilot who reaches the minimum of a rank but finds its places full falls to the best rank that is open to him.
  4. A tie is never split. Pilots with the same points hold the same rank. If the last place of a rank falls inside a tie, the whole tie takes the better rank, so a rank can hold more pilots than it has places, and never fewer than it should.

An example. The twelve best pilots of a company, with the rank each one holds:

PlacePvE pointsRank
160,000Senior Admiral
252,000Admiral
351,000Admiral
450,500Junior Admiral
544,000Junior Admiral
630,000Senior General
729,000General
828,000General
926,000Junior General
1024,999Senior Colonel
1121,000Colonel
121,000Senior Sergeant

Place 4 has 50,500 points, which reaches the Senior Admiral's minimum, but the Senior Admiral's one place and the Admirals' two are taken, so he is a Junior Admiral. Places 7 and 8 have 29,000 and 28,000: both reach the General's 27,500 and not the Senior General's 30,000, and the Generals have places left, so both are Generals. The pilot with 24,999 is a point short of a Junior General and is a Senior Colonel, the best rank open to him. If two pilots in the first places both had 60,000, both would be Senior Admirals, and the next two, with 50,000 and 45,000, the two Admirals.

Note

The places bind only when more pilots of a company reach a minimum than the rank has places. In a small company a rank is simply the points': a pilot alone in his company is a Colonel with 21,000 PvE points and a Senior Admiral with 50,000.

The 24 ranks

The places are how many pilots of one company can hold exactly this rank; a dash means no limit. The minimum is the least PvE points the rank asks for.

#RankPlaces per companyMinimum PvE points

19Junior General1525,000

22Junior Admiral440,000

24Senior Admiral150,000

Who is on the ladder

A pilot is on the ladder of his company when all three are true:

  • he is in a company;
  • he has PvE points: the first kill puts a new pilot on the ladder;
  • he has flown in the last 30 days.

A pilot who is not on the ladder is a Junior Pilot wherever a rank shows, has no place and is not in the company's list. The rule is there so that a pilot who tried the game once and left does not sit at the bottom for ever, and so that a pilot who is away cannot keep one of the few best places, or the crown, for months.

Tip

Nothing is lost while you are away. Your points are kept, and when you launch again, or just open the Company page, you are placed again with the points you left with, in the rank those points and the places of your company give you then.

If you change company, your points go with you and you stand on the ladder of the new company, with the rank its places give you there.

Your rank moves

  • Up to Senior Colonel it is your points' alone. It rises when your points reach the next minimum, as soon as your kill is counted, and no other pilot can lower it.
  • The six best ranks move with the other pilots of your company. A pilot who reaches a minimum before you takes one of the places, and when the places of your rank are full you drop to the next rank that is open to you. When a pilot leaves the ladder or the company, a place opens and the pilots behind him can rise into it.
  • A pilot with the same points as you or fewer never takes a place from you.
  • Your own rank is told to you when it rises, and only then (Promotions). A fall is never announced: your symbol just changes.

How you earn PvE points

Your PvE points are worked out from three things:

level × 100 + experience ÷ 1,000 (rounded down) + the points of every alien you destroyed

A tougher alien is worth more: a kill adds points by how much damage it takes to destroy the alien. The swarm ships and the Clan Wardens count by the same rule, so a Pirate Scout is worth as much as a Bulwark. Every kill is counted under the alien's own name in your kill statistics.

Alien or shipPvE points per kill
Seeker1
Phantasm2
Bulwark4
Goombah7
Crystalys16
Boss Seeker5
Seeker Slave1
Pirate Boss15
Pirate Scout4
Dormant Force25
Dormant Pulse11
Slumbering Void10
Inert Mass15
The Unwakened112
Brood Warden I, II, III14, 18, 35
Siege Warden I, II, III13, 17, 32
Wrath Warden I, II, III14, 18, 34
Brood Drone I, II, III1, 1, 2
Siege Escort I, II, III2, 3, 6
Wrath Guard I, II, III2, 3, 6

The first five rows are the regular aliens, the next six the ships of the three swarms and the next three the aliens of the Dormant Swamp (from season day 11). Last come the Clan Wardens, the leaders of a Clan Warden fight, and their crews, the Brood Drones, Siege Escorts and Wrath Guards: I, II and III are the Warden's strength, and the points of each are listed in that order.

For example, a pilot at level 4 with 12,500 experience who has destroyed 300 Seekers, 80 Phantasms and 10 Bulwarks has 400 + 12 + 300 + 160 + 40 = 912 points. That makes him a Sergeant: the minimum is 800, and the next rank, Senior Sergeant, asks 1,000. Up to Senior Colonel nothing but the points count.

The Rankings page (Community › Rankings) shows how your own points are made up, and the Hall of Fame on it lists the best pilots. The (i) next to the PvE points there lists the five aliens, what a kill in each of the swarms (Swarms) is worth, from its smallest ship to its boss, the same for the aliens of the Dormant Swamp, and the Clan Wardens.

The symbols

The game draws a rank as a small symbol: a shape for the tier, in a colour of its own, and one, two or three marks for the grade: one for a Junior, two for the plain rank, three for a Senior. The colours run from cool and plain to warm and bright as the tiers rise.

TierShapeColour
Pilotdotssteel blue
Sergeantchevrons, one above the othercopper
Lieutenantflat bars, one above the othersilver
Captaindiamondsgreen
Majorupward triangles (pennants)cyan
Colonelhollow ringsgold
Generalfive-pointed starsorange
Admirala laurel wreath open at the top, round one to three starsrose

The crown

The pilot with the most PvE points of the whole server wears a small gold crown over the symbol of his rank. "The whole server" means every company and all three worlds, not only your company: there is one crown on the server, and the best pilot of each company still holds the rank of his own. If several pilots have exactly the same points at the top, all of them wear it.

Only a pilot on a ladder can wear it. A pilot who has been away for 30 days does not, however many points he has: the crown goes to the best pilot who is on a ladder, and he gets it back when he flies again and is ahead. Nobody is told when the crown moves, you see it. It is not a rank and gives nothing: rest the pointer on a crowned symbol and its tip says "Top PvE pilot of the server".

Where you see them

In flight you see only the symbol, never the words. It stands before the pilot's name, and the crown over it, in all of these places:

  • over a ship, in the name tag, and in the Target window;
  • in the chat, before the name of the pilot who wrote the line;
  • in your group's list, and in the hover tip of a group mate on the minimap;
  • in the kill feed, before each pilot who is named (not before aliens);
  • in the Hall of Fame, in the Ranking window and, large, on a pilot's profile;
  • on the Company page: your own rank, the list of the best pilots and the table of all ranks.

The words (Junior Sergeant, Captain …) are on the Company page and in a hover tip: rest the pointer on a symbol. A symbol shows where a pilot stands among his own company's pilots, so the Major of another company is a Major among them, not among yours. Company pilots are the game's own squads and have no rank.

The company ranking

Open Economy › Company. Its Company ranking section shows, from the top:

  • Your rank: its symbol (with the crown, if it is yours) and name, your place ("Place 16 of 31") and a small tag with your percentile ("Top 52%").
  • A bar and a line under it that say what the next rank takes. A line like "2,500 PvE points to Junior General" says how many more PvE points the minimum of the next rank asks. When the next rank has no place free, the line names the pilot who holds the last one: "3,100 PvE points to pass Sable and reach Junior General". Matching his points is enough, because equal points hold the same rank. The Senior Admiral reads "The highest rank."
  • The best pilot of your company, with his points.
  • All ranks, shut until you open it: the 24 ranks, the best first, with their Places per company (a dash: no limit), the Pilots who hold each right now, with a bar as wide as the rank with the most of them, and the Min. points. Your own rank is marked, and a tip on a row says "Senior Admiral: 1 place per company, from 50,000 PvE points." A line under the table says who is on the ladder.
  • The list: the best 50 pilots of your company across all three worlds, with place, symbol, name and PvE points. Your own row is marked.
  • A pilot with no PvE points yet is not on the ladder and not in the list: destroy an alien to get on it. A pilot who has been away for 30 days is not on it either, until he launches or opens the page again.
  • Only names and public numbers are shown.

Promotions

  • When you reach a new best rank you get a toast ("Promoted: Senior Sergeant") and a short, quiet sound. "Best" means the best rank you have been told since you last launched: if you fall a grade and win it back, there is no second message. A rank you rose to while you were away is told once, at your next login. A fall is never told.
  • From Junior Major up, a promotion also shows in the chat's System tab for the pilots of your company who are flying in your world: "Nova was promoted to Junior Major." The company hears it only when your own PvE points lifted you; if you rose because other pilots left the ladder, you get your toast and nobody else is told.

Ranks and the wipe

A wipe changes nobody's points. It keeps your level, experience and kill statistics (Wipe Timeline), and your PvE points are worked out from them, so the ladder of your company is in the same order after the wipe, and so are the ranks and the crown. Your rank is not for life, though: the six best ranks move with the other pilots of your company, and a pilot who stays away for 30 days leaves the ladder until he flies again.

How long it takes

These are estimates from a model of how fast a pilot hunts, not measurements. A pilot who hunts about two hours a day, 58 hours in a season, has about 21,200 PvE points after one season: a Colonel. In hours of hunting, a Pilot's minimum comes inside the first hour, a Sergeant's in 4, a Captain's in 18, a Major's in 38, a Colonel's in 55, a Junior General's in 67, a General's in 73, a Senior General's in 78, a Junior Admiral's in 101, an Admiral's in 113 and the Senior Admiral's in 124.

So a typical active pilot reaches the ranks with places in his second season. Whether he gets a place is up to the other pilots of his company, who hunt too: the places of a rank matter only once more pilots reach its minimum than it has places. Until then the rank is simply your points'.

The **(i)** next to the PvE points there lists the five aliens, what a kill in each of the swarms ([Swarms](/wiki/05-Swarms/Swarms.md)) is worth, from its smallest ship to its boss, the same for the aliens of the [Dormant Swamp](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Dormant-Swamp.md), and the [Clan Wardens](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Clans.md#clan-wardens).

## The symbols

The game draws a rank as a small symbol: a **shape** for the tier, in a colour of its own, and **one, two or three marks** for the grade: one for a Junior, two for the plain rank, three for a Senior. The colours run from cool and plain to warm and bright as the tiers rise.

| Tier | Shape | Colour |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Pilot | dots | steel blue |
| Sergeant | chevrons, one above the other | copper |
| Lieutenant | flat bars, one above the other | silver |
| Captain | diamonds | green |
| Major | upward triangles (pennants) | cyan |
| Colonel | hollow rings | gold |
| General | five-pointed stars | orange |
| Admiral | a laurel wreath open at the top, round one to three stars | rose |

## The crown

The pilot with the **most PvE points of the whole server** wears a small **gold crown** over the symbol of his rank. "The whole server" means every company and all three worlds, not only your company: there is one crown on the server, and the best pilot of each company still holds the rank of his own. If several pilots have exactly the same points at the top, all of them wear it.

Only a pilot on a ladder can wear it. A pilot who has been away for 30 days does not, however many points he has: the crown goes to the best pilot who is on a ladder, and he gets it back when he flies again and is ahead. Nobody is told when the crown moves, you see it. It is not a rank and gives nothing: rest the pointer on a crowned symbol and its tip says "Top PvE pilot of the server".

## Where you see them

In flight you see **only the symbol**, never the words. It stands before the pilot's name, and the crown over it, in all of these places:

- over a ship, in the name tag, and in the Target window;
- in the chat, before the name of the pilot who wrote the line;
- in your group's list, and in the hover tip of a group mate on the minimap;
- in the kill feed, before each pilot who is named (not before aliens);
- in the Hall of Fame, in the Ranking window and, large, on a pilot's profile;
- on the Company page: your own rank, the list of the best pilots and the table of all ranks.

The **words** (Junior Sergeant, Captain …) are on the Company page and in a hover tip: rest the pointer on a symbol. A symbol shows where a pilot stands among **his own company's** pilots, so the Major of another company is a Major among them, not among yours. [Company pilots](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Company-Pilots.md) are the game's own squads and have no rank.

## The company ranking

Open **Economy › Company**. Its **Company ranking** section shows, from the top:

- **Your rank**: its symbol (with the crown, if it is yours) and name, your place ("Place 16 of 31") and a small tag with your percentile ("Top 52%").
- **A bar and a line under it** that say what the next rank takes. A line like "2,500 PvE points to Junior General" says how many more PvE points the minimum of the next rank asks. When the next rank has no place free, the line names the pilot who holds the last one: "3,100 PvE points to pass Sable and reach Junior General". Matching his points is enough, because equal points hold the same rank. The Senior Admiral reads "The highest rank."
- **The best pilot** of your company, with his points.
- **All ranks**, shut until you open it: the 24 ranks, the best first, with their **Places** per company (a dash: no limit), the **Pilots** who hold each right now, with a bar as wide as the rank with the most of them, and the **Min. points**. Your own rank is marked, and a tip on a row says "Senior Admiral: 1 place per company, from 50,000 PvE points." A line under the table says who is on the ladder.
- **The list**: the best **50 pilots of your company across all three worlds**, with place, symbol, name and PvE points. Your own row is marked.

- A pilot with no PvE points yet is not on the ladder and not in the list: destroy an alien to get on it. A pilot who has been away for 30 days is not on it either, until he launches or opens the page again.
- Only names and public numbers are shown.

## Promotions

- When you reach a new best rank you get a toast ("Promoted: Senior Sergeant") and a short, quiet sound. "Best" means the best rank you have been told since you last launched: if you fall a grade and win it back, there is no second message. A rank you rose to while you were away is told once, at your next login. A fall is never told.
- From **Junior Major** up, a promotion also shows in the chat's **System** tab for the pilots of your company who are flying in your world: "Nova was promoted to Junior Major." The company hears it only when your own PvE points lifted you; if you rose because other pilots left the ladder, you get your toast and nobody else is told.

## Ranks and the wipe

A wipe changes nobody's points. It keeps your level, experience and kill statistics ([Wipe Timeline](/wiki/03-Mechanics/Wipe-Timeline.md#cross-season-progression-permanent-buffs-)), and your PvE points are worked out from them, so the ladder of your company is in the same order after the wipe, and so are the ranks and the crown. Your rank is not for life, though: the six best ranks move with the other pilots of your company, and a pilot who stays away for 30 days leaves the ladder until he flies again.

## How long it takes

These are **estimates** from a model of how fast a pilot hunts, not measurements. A pilot who hunts about two hours a day, 58 hours in a season, has about 21,200 PvE points after one season: a Colonel. In hours of hunting, a Pilot's minimum comes inside the first hour, a Sergeant's in 4, a Captain's in 18, a Major's in 38, a Colonel's in 55, a Junior General's in 67, a General's in 73, a Senior General's in 78, a Junior Admiral's in 101, an Admiral's in 113 and the Senior Admiral's in 124.

So a typical active pilot reaches the ranks with places in his second season. Whether he gets a place is up to the other pilots of his company, who hunt too: the places of a rank matter only once more pilots reach its minimum than it has places. Until then the rank is simply your points'.

research.title: Research
research.html:
The Research Centre is the laboratory of your Skylab. You feed it resources, it turns them into science, and the science researches technologies. Every craft in Assembly needs its technology first: a ship, a laser, a thruster or a CPU cannot be made until it has been researched.

This page has the whole technology tree with the time each technology takes, the science each resource gives, the Thulium boost, the rule for Dark Matter and the new CPUs. Its numbers are read from the game's own data, so they are always the ones in the game.

The Research Centre

  • Unlocks at Core level 10. The Research Centre is a module of your Skylab, built like the others: 25 Ship Fragments from your inventory (with your ship landed), 25,000 Credits and 500 Thulium. Its screen is the Research view of the Skylab page.
  • Levels 1 to 10. A higher level gives a bigger tank and draws more power. It does not make research faster: a technology takes the same time at every level.
  • The tank. The Centre keeps its science in a tank that holds 12 h of research at level 1 and 25% more with every level (the table below).
  • Fuel into science. A resource you feed becomes science at once, as the fuel table shows. A research burns 1 science for every second of its research time; with the tank empty it waits, and it goes on when you feed the Centre.
  • A free first hour. A new Centre starts with 3,600 science in its tank, 1 h of research.
  • One at a time. The Centre researches one technology at a time, but you can line up to 5 more behind it with the Queue button. Each one starts by itself the moment the one before it finishes, even while you are away. Nothing is paid when you queue: a technology takes its Dark Matter when it starts, and a queued one can be taken out again for free.
  • While you are away. A research runs on the server's clock, so it goes on after you log out, until it is finished or the tank is empty. A blackout or an upgrade of the Centre does not stop it.
  • Power. The Centre draws 25 at level 1 and 15% more with every level, and it cannot be switched off.
  • The wipe keeps all of it: your technologies, the science in the tank, the Dark Matter plugged in, a research under way and the boost.
  • What you own is yours. When research came into the game, every pilot received the technology of each item they already held, and the technologies those needed. An item that reaches you later (a gift, a code, a reward) does not unlock its technology, with one exception: an Engine II, an Engine III, an Adaptive Core II or an Adaptive Core III that a code, a quest, an invitation or an administrator gives you unlocks its technology, and the ones it needs, at once.
  • Below Core level 10 you cannot research, so you cannot make anything new in Assembly yet. The Station missions walk you up the Core.

The laser amps and the last tier. The Damage, Crit and Penetration Amps of tiers II to IV are researched crafts like the rest. Pilots who held or had queued amps when the amp families came received the technology of each of those amps and of the tiers below them. Thirteen technologies need a technology of another tree, the Dark Matter Plate's of the Resources tree, because the last tier of every upgrade chain asks for three plates: the tier IV Damage, Crit and Penetration Amps, the tier IV Absorption and Capacity Shield Cells, the tier IV Impulse and Momentum Thrusters, the Heavy Shield Core, the Engine III, the Adaptive Core III, the Helios Beam, the Extra Slots CPU III and the Base CPU II. A pilot who researched one of them earlier keeps it, and needs the plate's technology to craft its plates. The tree below draws no arrow for it, but the table lists it and the card in the game names it (Dark Matter and Dark Matter Plates).

In the Research view of your Skylab a technology tells you more than a box of the trees below. Point at one and a card opens with the research time and the science it burns and, under them, what the item is and does: its kind and its tier in its family (for example the third of the four Impulse Thrusters), its description, its numbers as the Hangar and the Shop show them (the damage, crit chance and range of a laser, the capacity, recharge and absorbance of a shield, the speed boost and multiplier of a thruster, the damage, blast and range of a rocket, what a drone formation gives and what it costs you), a small table of the tiers of its family, and what Assembly then asks to craft it: the time, the Credits and Thulium and the materials. So you can see what a tier gives before you research it. Click a technology to pick it: the card beside the tree shows the same in full, under the Start research button. While a research runs, Queue takes the place of the Start button: a queued technology shows its order number on the tree, and a queue card under the research that runs lists them all, each with a cross to take it out. If the next one cannot start (the Dark Matter it needs is not in the Centre, or the tank is empty), the queue waits and says why, until you fix it and press Start queue.

Fuel

You feed the Centre with resources, and each unit becomes science at once. The more work a unit takes to get, the more science it gives: the figures follow how hard a unit is to get, not its rarity label. The ores are the exception: a unit gives more science than the seconds a collector takes to mine it, so an hour of the ore of a collector in the middle of its levels feeds about two hours of research. The ores come from the Resource Storage of your Skylab, and the Ore Bay moves the Velkonite and the Orvium of your inventory (a giant excavator's boxes) there; every other resource comes from your inventory, and your ship must be landed. The Velkonite Reinforced Plate, the Orvium Reinforced Plate, the Dark Matter Plate, Dark Matter, Credits and Thulium cannot be burnt; the Reinforced Hull Plate can.

The last column is the number of units that run one hour of research without the boost, rounded up; with the boost it is 2 times as many.

The Thulium boost

  • 5,000 Thulium buys a boost: the Centre researches 2 times faster for 24 hours.
  • It also burns science 2 times as fast, so a boost buys time and never fuel: a technology burns the same science, boosted or not.
  • A boost starts the moment you buy it and runs on the clock whether the tank has fuel or not, so buy it while a research is running. The Centre refuses one when nothing is being researched.
  • Boosts add up: buying one while another runs adds 24 hours to its end, up to 72 hours ahead. A boost belongs to your Research Centre, not to one research.

Dark Matter

The technologies at the top of the tree need Dark Matter as well. It comes from the black hole, where a N.I.K.E. rocket that reaches it leaves some, and now and then from a Pulse of the Dormant Swarm.

  • 10 Dark Matter for each of the 16 technologies in the table below, on top of the science: plug it into the Research Centre (from your inventory, with your ship landed) before you start, and the research takes it when it starts.
  • The rule: an item of rarity Epic or higher whose research takes 10 h or more. The N.I.K.E., which is how Dark Matter is made, never needs it.
  • Drone formations are outside the rule: every formation research asks Dark Matter, 5, 13 or 20 by strength, as the table shows.
  • Hull Plating is outside the rule too: its two researches ask more, 25 Dark Matter for a day of research and 40 for two days, as the table shows.
  • Cancel a research and the Dark Matter you plugged in for it comes back to the Centre. The progress and the science already burnt do not.
  • All of them together ask 414 Dark Matter.

Each box is a technology: the item it lets you make, with its research time under the name (the clock) and, where it needs Dark Matter, the Dark Matter badge. The CPUs

The new CPUs are researched here too, then made in Assembly. The same table and notes are on the Extras page.

None of them is sold in the Shop: research the technology, then make the CPU in Assembly. Point at a CPU in its tree to see what Assembly asks for it.

Extra Slots CPUs

  • What they do. Extra Slots CPU I, II and III give every ship 3, 5 and 7 more extra slots, so 6, 8 and 10 in all on a ship that has 3 of its own, and 5, 7 and 9 on one that has 2. A higher CPU replaces the one before it: II does not add to I.
  • Installed, not carried. An Extra Slots CPU is not an item: when you collect it in Assembly it installs itself in your Skylab, for every ship in both configurations, and it takes no slot. It stays through the wipe.
  • In order. Craft them one after the other: II only when I is installed, III only when II is installed; until then Assembly tells you which one to install first. The three cost 117,000 Thulium in all: 12,000, 30,000 and 75,000.

Jump CPU

  • What it does. It jumps your ship to any company sector of your world, your own company's and the other companies' alike, their home sectors included (M, T and G, sectors 1 to 4), for 500 Thulium a jump. It has no limit on uses: you only pay the Thulium. It never goes to a Danger Sector (DS) or a neutral sector (N).
  • The jump. Press the JMP slot, pick the sector on the Star System map and confirm: the ship charges for 5 seconds, then arrives at a gate of that sector, protected as after any gate jump. The CPU cools down for 30 seconds after you arrive.
  • Not in a fight. It cannot start within 10 seconds of firing or being hit, and a shot or a hit while it charges cancels the jump; nothing is paid then. You cannot jump while cloaked.
  • Not from a neutral sector: a pilot in a neutral sector, or with no company, cannot use it.
  • It may leave a Danger Sector when you are not in a fight.

Base CPUs

  • What they do. They teleport your ship to the base of your company, into the safe zone around its station (M-1, T-1 or G-1, the sector with Mission Control), free of Thulium. You start them from the BSE slot of the hotbar.
  • Not in a fight. A charge of 10 seconds, the same for both. It cannot start within 10 seconds of firing or being hit, while you are cloaked or when you are already inside the safe zone of your base, and a shot or a hit while it charges cancels it.
CPUUsesCooldown
Base CPU I1010 min
Base CPU II255 min
  • Used up, not recharged. Each use takes one of the CPU's uses, and a CPU with none left is gone: craft a new one. With both fitted, the better one (II) is used first.

Auto-Repair CPU

  • What it does. It sends out the Repair Drone fitted in your extra slots by itself, whenever you could have sent it out by hand: your hull is not full, the drone is not already out and 10 seconds have passed since the last hit. There is no hull level to set.
  • It takes an extra slot of its own and does nothing without a Repair Drone in an extra slot of the same configuration. It never sends out a Repair Drone in an ability slot (that one is the Emergency Repair button).
  • If you stop the drone by hand, the CPU leaves it alone until your hull is full again, or until you send the drone out yourself.
